title: Screen time and manic symptoms in early adolescents: prospective findings from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
authors: Nagata JM, Zamora G, Al-Shoaibi AAA, Lavender JM, Ganson KT, Testa A, He J, Baker FC

primary_models.name: Multivariable linear regression (robust SE) of Year 3 manic symptoms on Year 1 phone/SM screen time, adjusted for Year 1 manic, ADHD and depressive symptoms
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, Model 2 (Adjusted) (p. 1484); results text p. 1482; interpreted in Discussion p. 1483 and Conclusions p. 1485
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Screen time measured at the Year 1 follow-up (2017-2019, ages 10-11); manic symptoms measured at the Year 3 follow-up. Single follow-up outcome, one observation per participant, no repeated measures. Year 1 manic symptom score enters as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with Year 3 symptoms net of Year 1 symptoms. No time-by-IV interaction. Each screen subtype was entered in a separate model (one IV per model).
primary_models.sample: ABCD 5.0 release, Year 1, Year 2 and Year 3 follow-ups. Of 11,875 participants, 1,828 were missing Year 3 manic symptoms and 804 were missing Year 1 covariates, leaving N=9,243 (same N for all Table 2 estimates). Mean age 10.9 (SD 0.6) at Year 1; 48.8% female, 51.2% male; 56.0% White, 19.1% Latino/Hispanic, 14.4% Black, 5.3% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 2.0% Other (44.0% racial/ethnic minority); 50.2% household income below $75,000; 89.5% parent with college education or more. Table 1 descriptives are propensity-weighted.
primary_models.iv: Typical daily screen time (hours/day) at Year 1 from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, one subtype per model. Qualifying subtypes: texting, video chatting (e.g., Skype, FaceTime), and social media (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). Weekday and weekend reports combined as [(weekday average x 5) + (weekend average x 2)]/7. Table 1 (weighted) Year 1 means: texting 0.4 (SD 0.7), video chat 0.3 (SD 0.6), social media 0.2 (SD 0.6) h/day. Continuous; coefficient is per 1 hour/day.
primary_models.dv: Year 3 manic symptoms: youth-report 7 Up subscale (7 items) of the 7 Up 7 Down Inventory, each item 0 (never) to 3 (very often or almost constantly), summed to a total score (range 0-21); alpha=0.77. Year 3 mean 1.9 (SD 2.5) (Table 1); 0.8% scored at or above the proposed clinical cutoff of 11.

primary_models.equation: Mania_Y3[i] = b0 + b1*ScreenSubtype_Y1[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4..b8*race_ethnicity + b9*income_lt75k + b10*parent_ed + b11*site + b12*Mania_Y1 + b13*ADHD_T_Y1 + b14*Depressive_T_Y1 + b15*covid_timeframe + e[i]; fitted separately for each screen subtype (texting, video chat, social media; also overall, TV, videos, video games which are excluded here).
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18.0. Multivariable linear regression with robust standard errors. Propensity weighting based on the American Community Survey (US Census) applied for representative population estimates. Two-sided p<0.05 for significance. No multiple-comparison correction reported. No sex or race interaction tests or stratified results reported. Sensitivity analyses (cross-sectional Year 3 associations, Supplemental Table 1; logistic regression on binary clinical cutoff of manic symptoms, Supplemental Table 2) are referenced but the supplement is not bundled in this PDF.

estimates.note: Lower CI bound printed to three decimals (-0.012) in the table. Unadjusted Model 1: 0.38 (0.27, 0.49), p<0.001.

primary_models.name: Generalized SEM mediation of Year 3 manic symptoms on Year 1 social media time via Year 2 problematic social media use, adjusted for covariates
primary_models.location_in_paper: Fig. 1 (p. 1484); results text p. 1482; proportion mediated reported in text p. 1482 (Supplementary Table 3); interpreted in Discussion p. 1485
primary_models.design: Prospective three-wave mediation. Social media time at Year 1 (X), problematic social media use (SMAQ) at Year 2 (M), manic symptoms at Year 3 (Y). Single observation per participant. Reports total-effect decomposition into a direct effect (X to Y net of M) and an indirect effect (X to M to Y).
primary_models.sample: Described as the same ABCD 5.0 analytic sample as M1 (N=9,243); the paper does not print a separate N for the mediation model. SMAQ was completed by 4,938 participants with at least one social media account; those without a social media account were assigned 1 (Never) on each item.
primary_models.iv: Typical daily social media time at Year 1 (hours/day), same measure as M1; Table 1 mean 0.2 (SD 0.6).
primary_models.dv: Year 3 manic symptoms (7 Up subscale sum score), same as M1; Table 1 mean 1.9 (SD 2.5). Mediator: Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ) at Year 2, 6 items on a 1-6 Likert scale, sum score range 6-36, alpha=0.89; Table 1 mean 6.2 (SD 6.7).

covariates.name: Same covariates as M1
covariates.detail: Text states 'Adjusting for covariates' for the mediation; the paper does not separately list them for the SEM. Presumably age, sex, race/ethnicity, household income, parent education, study site, Year 1 manic, ADHD and depressive symptoms, and COVID timeframe.

primary_models.equation: SMAQ_Y2[i] = a0 + a*SocialMedia_Y1[i] + covariates + e1[i]; Mania_Y3[i] = c0 + c'*SocialMedia_Y1[i] + b*SMAQ_Y2[i] + covariates + e2[i]; indirect effect = a*b; proportion mediated = a*b / (a*b + c').
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18.0 generalized structural equation modeling with maximum likelihood estimation. Bias-corrected 95% CIs for the indirect effect from 5000 bootstrap samples; significance if the CI excludes zero. ACS propensity weighting applied to analyses. Two-sided p<0.05. Path coefficients are labeled beta in Fig. 1 but reported as B in text; the paper does not state they are standardized. Figure path values: a (social media to problematic SM use) = 2.23***, b (problematic SM use to manic symptoms) = 0.06***.

dv_axis.label: Manic symptoms (Year 3): indirect effect via Year 2 problematic SM use

estimates.note: Indirect effect (a*b) with bias-corrected bootstrap CI. Proportion mediated 47.7% (95% CI 23.3%, 72.0%), p<0.001 (text p. 1482, Supplementary Table 3).

excluded_models.why: a path pairs two phone/SM variables (no trait on the other side); b path has SMAQ as a mediator, which does not qualify under FT-IC2 clarification 7. Values (2.23***, 0.06***) recorded in M2 estimation text; only star-coded significance, no CIs.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). Apply to B, B_lo and B_hi.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 hour/day of the Year 1 screen subtype (native); per 1 SD of the IV after conversion
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 1483), Year 1 typical hours/day, propensity-weighted: texting 0.7, video chat 0.6, social media 0.6. SD_DV = 2.5, Year 3 manic symptoms (7 Up) from Table 1 (p. 1483). Table 1 descriptives are weighted estimates, not unweighted analytic-sample SDs. The M2 indirect effect is a product term (a*b); converting it with the same beta_std formula is an approximation and the bootstrap CI is not symmetric. Converted d values will be small (e.g., social media M1: beta_std = 0.20*0.6/2.5 = 0.048). Not directly comparable to papers using high vs. low group contrasts. Verification pass (2026-10-01): re-read all 9 pages; every B, CI and SD in M1 and M2 matches Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 1 and Results text; no native values or SDs were missing. iv_type set to continuous for both models. p for texting (M1) and the M2 indirect effect is printed only as <0.001 (kept in p_label).

extraction_flags: 1) The PDF has no supplement. Supplemental Tables 1 (cross-sectional Y3) and 2 (logistic regression on the clinical cutoff) may contain per-subtype texting, video chat and social media estimates, and someone should check the online supplement. 2) SD_IV and SD_DV come from Table 1, which is propensity-weighted, so they are not unweighted analytic-sample SDs. The social media IV is heavily floored (M 0.2, SD 0.6). 3) For the M2 mediation, the covariates are only described as "adjusting for covariates". I assumed the M1 set and flagged that in the file. The paths are labeled beta in Fig. 1 but B in the text, and nothing says they are standardized. The p-value for the indirect effect is <0.001 only. Converting the indirect effect (a*b) to d is approximate. 4) The paper is inconsistent about the sleep mediation: the abstract and results text say video game screen time, while Fig. 3 and the Methods say total screen time. It is excluded either way. 5) The video chat lower CI bound is printed as -0.012 (three decimals) in Table 2. 6) Study site is listed as an adjustment variable, and it is unclear whether it was a fixed or random effect.
